short: Inquiring into the nature of the 'I' until its source is recognised.
beginner: Self-inquiry means turning attention back on yourself and asking 'Who am I?' — not as a puzzle to solve with thoughts, but as a way of looking for the one who is aware of thoughts.
what: Atma-vichara is the practice of investigating the nature of the Self. In Advaita Vedanta, inquiry (vichara) is a sustained reflection on scripture and experience that distinguishes the Self from body, mind and ego. Ramana Maharshi made a direct form of it central: tracing the 'I'-thought back to its source rather than analysing ideas about the self. Related approaches include the neti-neti method of the Upanishads and the discrimination between seer and seen.
scholar: Shankara's tradition speaks of shravana (hearing), manana (reflection) and nididhyasana (contemplation) as the process of knowledge. Texts traditionally attributed to Shankara, such as Vivekachudamani and Aparokshanubhuti, and later works like Drg-drshya-viveka, elaborate vichara. Ramana Maharshi's Nan Yar (Who Am I?) and Upadesa Saram present inquiry as attending to the 'I'-sense until it subsides in its source; scholars note both continuity with and distinctness from classical Advaita.

perspectives.view: Advaita holds that liberation comes through knowledge, and self-inquiry, guided by scripture and a teacher, removes the superimposition of the non-self on the Self.
Ramana Maharshi taught a direct inquiry into the source of the 'I'-thought, presented as open to anyone regardless of background; this is a twentieth-century teaching.
Pratyabhijna offers a related but distinct approach: recognising that one's own awareness is Shiva, understood as dynamic and self-reflective rather than inactive.

follow.note: The body is the 'field'; the one who knows it is the knower of the field.
